name: Seletinoid G

lead: Seletinoid G is an experimental retinoid designed with computer modelling by Korean researchers to treat aged skin with less irritation than tretinoin. The payoff sought is fewer wrinkles and smoother skin from retinoid-style renewal at a gentler level.

As a retinoid it is meant to act on skin cells to influence extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen. Human data are a 2005 experiment in 23 volunteers using occlusive application on the buttocks for four days, plus 2020 skin-model work on barrier function and wound healing. No patient trials are known.

paras: It is not a marketed approved drug, so there is no standard routine. It appears in research on topical anti-aging and skin-barrier repair.
Its stated aim was lower irritation than tretinoin, based on the small 2005 comparison. It has no approved status and no long-term safety data were found.

angle.text: Seletinoid G is a lab-designed retinoid intended to renew aged and photoaged skin with less irritation than tretinoin, aiming for fewer wrinkles and smoother skin. Human data come from a 23-person, four-day study plus skin-model work.

lead: Seletinoid G is an experimental synthetic retinoid designed by Korean researchers with computer-aided molecular modelling as a topical anti-aging ingredient. The aim was a molecule that keeps the skin-renewing activity of retinoids, which can smooth wrinkles and improve texture in aged and sun-damaged skin, while causing less of the redness and irritation that often limits all-trans retinoic acid (tretinoin).[1]

In the 2005 human study, seletinoid G raised procollagen, tropoelastin and fibrillin-1 in skin and reduced the collagen-degrading enzyme MMP-1, with no irritation, whereas the tretinoin comparator irritated the skin.[1][2] Later laboratory work in 2020 reported that it increased keratinocyte proliferation and migration, sped wound closure and restored collagen that UVB had reduced in human skin equivalents.[3][2]
It is not an approved drug, and the published human evidence is a small short-term experiment rather than a trial of visible wrinkle improvement.[1][2]

paras: Seletinoid G has been investigated as a cosmetic-type active for aged skin. The stated rationale in its 2005 report was that retinoids have potential efficacy in aged skin but that skin irritation limits their use, and that a newly designed molecule might keep the activity with less irritation.[1] Retinoid reviews describe tretinoin as having the strongest antiaging evidence and cosmetic retinoids such as retinol as lacking well-designed trials, which frames the interest in alternatives.[2]

As a retinoid, it is studied for effects on extracellular matrix proteins: in the 2005 experiment, it increased procollagen, tropoelastin and fibrillin-1 and reduced MMP-1, and countered UV-induced collagen loss.[2] In the 2020 laboratory study, it increased keratinocyte proliferation and migration and restored collagen in UVB-exposed skin equivalents, examined with optical coherence tomography and second harmonic generation imaging.[3][2]

Laboratory work has examined its effects on keratinocyte-mediated wound closure and collagen organisation in skin models, framed by the authors as relevant to anti-aging because wound healing is impaired in older skin.[3] A separate 2019 paper by Park and Cho tested kojyl cinnamate ester derivatives on adiponectin and hair growth factors in cell models and used seletinoid G only as a reference compound, in which the derivatives outperformed it at inducing adiponectin; it is not evidence about seletinoid G as a hair treatment.[4][2]

A 2005 study in Clinica Chimica Acta by Kim and colleagues tested seletinoid G against all-trans retinoic acid in 23 volunteers, applying each for four days under occlusion on the buttocks and measuring erythema, blood flow and matrix proteins in biopsies; seletinoid G caused no irritation, unlike the comparator.[1][2] It is a short mechanistic experiment rather than a trial of visible wrinkle improvement on the face.
The 2020 work used human skin equivalents rather than patients.[3] No randomised controlled trials in patients were found.

timeline.event: Kim and colleagues report the first human experiment of seletinoid G in 23 volunteers.[1]
Lee and colleagues report skin-equivalent studies of wound healing and collagen realignment.[3]
